procedural_history.originating_court: Magistrate Court (issuing summons for trial u/ss.406, 504 and 506, Penal Code, 1860 in Criminal Complaint Case No.7990 of 2020 via summoning order issued on 18.08.2021)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 23.03.2023 of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in A482 No.18603 of 2021.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed Criminal Miscellaneous Application No.18603/2021 before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad under Section 482 of the 1973 Code to quash the summons issued by the Magistrate and the complaint case itself. The High Court dismissed the application on 23.03.2023, reasoning that the complaint involved adjudication of disputed questions of fact and refrained from considering the defence of the accused.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed the High Court's judgment to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and quashed the Criminal Complaint Case No.7990 of 2020 and the summoning order issued on 18.08.2021. The Supreme Court found that the Magistrate failed to apply his mind in issuing summons and the High Court also failed to exercise its jurisdiction under Section 482 of the 1973 Code to prevent abuse of the power of the Criminal Court.

directions: Quash the Criminal Complaint Case No.7990 of 2020.
Quash the summoning order issued on 18.08.2021.
All consequential steps in connection with the said proceeding shall stand quashed.

issue.issue_text: In a case wherein the dispute was commercial in nature having no element of criminality, whether the Magistrate was justified in issuing summons for trial u/ss.406, 504 and 506, Penal Code, 1860 and the High Court in dismissing the application filed by the appellant for quashing said summons and the complaint case.

facts: The underlying dispute between the parties was purely commercial in nature, related to the rate at which assigned work was to be done.

This commercial dispute was given a "criminal colour" by filing a complaint alleging offenses under sections 406 (criminal breach of trust), 504 (intentional insult), and 506 (criminal intimidation) of the Penal Code.
A Magistrate issued summons for trial based on this complaint.

The appellant filed an application in the High Court to quash the summons and the complaint, but the High Court dismissed it, stating that the case involved disputed questions of fact and that the appellant could seek discharge later in the trial.
law: When issuing a summons, a Magistrate must be satisfied not only that there is a prima facie case, but also that there are "sufficient grounds for proceeding."
A civil dispute, such as a breach of contract, should not be converted into a criminal offense by simply lifting words and phrases from the penal code and inserting them into a complaint.
The High Court has the jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash criminal proceedings to prevent an abuse of the court's process.
When a complaint does not disclose any criminal offense at all, the proceedings should be quashed, and the accused should not be forced to undergo a trial.
application: The Supreme Court found that the allegations made in the complaint did not actually give rise to the criminal offenses for which the appellant was summoned.
It noted there was no evidence for the offense of criminal breach of trust (s.406) and that the allegation of criminal intimidation (s.506) was a "mere bald allegation" without necessary details.

The Court concluded that the Magistrate had failed to properly apply his mind to determine if there were sufficient grounds for a criminal proceeding, instead accepting a complaint that improperly framed a commercial dispute as a criminal one.

The Supreme Court held that the High Court was wrong to dismiss the quashing application. It should have exercised its jurisdiction to quash the proceedings because "no case at all has been made out," and allowing the criminal case to continue would be an abuse of the legal process.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the decisions of the lower courts, finding that both the Magistrate and the High Court were unjustified. The Court held that the dispute was entirely commercial and had been improperly converted into a criminal case. It concluded that the Magistrate failed to apply his mind before issuing the summons, and the High Court failed in its duty to quash a baseless criminal proceeding. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and quashed the criminal complaint and the summoning order.

arguments.issue_text: In a case wherein the dispute was commercial in nature having no element of criminality, whether the Magistrate was justified in issuing summons for trial u/ss.406, 504 and 506, Penal Code, 1880 and the High Court in dismissing the application filed by the appellant for quashing said summons and the complaint case.
appellant_arguments: The dispute is essentially a civil dispute arising from a breach of contract and does not constitute a criminal offence of cheating or criminal breach of trust (s.406).
For a criminal offence to be made out, there must be an intention to cheat from the very inception, which is absent in this case.

The allegation of criminal intimidation (s.506) is a 'mere bald allegation' and a 'reproduction of part of the statutory provision,' lacking any specific particulars about how the threat was conveyed.
The allegations, even when taken at face value and accepted in their entirety, do not prima facie constitute any offence or make out a case against the accused.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's specific arguments are not detailed in the provided text. However, their position, by instituting the complaint and opposing the quashing petition, was that the appellant's actions constituted the criminal offences of criminal breach of trust (s.406), intentional insult (s.504), and criminal intimidation (s.506), thereby justifying the summons issued by the Magistrate and the High Court's refusal to quash the proceedings.

cases.case_name: Prof. R.K. Vijayasarathy and Anr. -vs- Sudha Seetharam and Anr.
cases.principle: To support the view that criminal proceedings should be quashed when the dispute is essentially civil or commercial in nature and the ingredients of the criminal offence are not made out.

cases.case_name: Vijay Kumar Ghai and Ors. -vs- State of West Bengal and Ors.
cases.principle: To support the view that criminal proceedings should be quashed when the dispute is essentially civil or commercial in nature and the ingredients of the criminal offence are not made out.

cases.case_name: Dalip Kaur and Ors. -vs- Jagnar Singh and Anr.
cases.principle: For the test to be applied to determine if the materials on record disclose the commission of an offence for criminal breach of trust under Section 405/406 IPC.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A criminal proceeding is liable to be quashed if the allegations, taken at face value and accepted in their entirety, do not prima facie constitute any offense, or where there is no legal evidence adduced in support of the case, or the evidence manifestly fails to prove the charge.
obiter: A Magistrate is empowered to take cognizance if the material on record provides sufficient ground for proceeding, not whether there is sufficient ground for conviction.

The essential elements to constitute an offense of criminal breach of trust are: entrustment with property or dominion over it; dishonest misappropriation or conversion of that property; and such action being in violation of a legal direction or contract.
A criminal proceeding can be quashed where there is an express legal bar to its institution and continuance.
In exercising its inherent jurisdiction, the High Court should not embark upon an enquiry as to whether the evidence is reliable, as that is the function of the trial Magistrate.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's core finding is that a dispute that is essentially civil in nature, arising from a breach of contract, cannot be converted into a criminal offense of cheating or criminal breach of trust without clear evidence of dishonest intent from the very inception. The court, referencing its decision in Binod Kumar, found that the essential ingredients of criminal breach of trust or a dishonest intention of inducement, which must form the foundation of the complaint, were missing. A mere failure to refund an amount as per a contract does not, by itself, constitute a criminal offense.
legal_tests_applied: The test for criminal breach of trust under Section 405 of the Penal Code, which requires the presence of three elements: (a) the accused was entrusted with property, or with dominion over property; (b) the accused had dishonestly misappropriated or converted that property to their own use; and (c) such misappropriation or conversion was in violation of any direction of law or legal contract.

The test for determining if a breach of contract constitutes cheating, which requires the court to pose the question "as to whether any act of inducement on the part of the appellant has been raised by the second respondent and whether the appellant had an intention to cheat him from the very inception."

The standard for quashing a criminal complaint, specifically where "the uncontroverted allegations made in the FIR or complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same do not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case against the accused."
policy_considerations: The judgment implicitly reinforces the policy of preventing the misuse of the criminal justice system to settle disputes that are fundamentally civil or commercial in nature. By quashing the criminal complaint, the court maintains a clear distinction between a civil liability arising from a breach of contract and criminal culpability, which requires a specific criminal intent (mens rea) from the outset, thereby preventing criminal proceedings from being used as a tool for commercial recovery or to exert pressure in civil disputes.
